name: Charyn Canyon
description: Charyn Canyon stretches for about 150 km along the Charyn River and is part of Charyn National Park (created in 2004). Its most famous section, the Valley of Castles, is a 2-3 km walk between red sandstone walls shaped by wind and water into towers and 'castles'. The trail ends at the river, where there is a small eco-camp. The canyon is often compared to a smaller Grand Canyon and is one of the most popular day trips from Almaty.
how_to_get_there: About 3-4 hours by car from Almaty along the road towards Kegen. There is no regular public transport to the canyon itself, so most visitors go with a tour group, a rented car or a hired driver. Organised tours often combine Charyn with Kolsai and Kaindy lakes in a 1-2 day trip.
tips: Summer afternoons are very hot and there is little shade, so start early and bring at least 2 litres of water per person. Wear closed shoes. The national park charges a small entrance fee. Spring (April-May) and autumn (September-October) have the most comfortable temperatures.

name: Kolsai Lakes
description: The Kolsai Lakes are a chain of three mountain lakes in the Northern Tien Shan, protected by Kolsai Lakes National Park. The lower lake (about 1,800 m above sea level) is reachable by car; the middle lake is a hike of roughly 8-9 km (3-4 hours) through spruce forest, and the upper lake lies close to the border with Kyrgyzstan. The area is known as the 'pearls of the Tien Shan' and is great for hiking, horse riding and camping.
how_to_get_there: About 5-6 hours by car from Almaty via the villages of Saty or Kurmenty. Guest houses in Saty village are a convenient base. Many tour operators run 2-day tours combining Kolsai, Kaindy and Charyn.
tips: Nights are cold even in summer, so bring warm clothes. Stay in a guest house in Saty and start the hike to the middle lake early. Hiking beyond the middle lake towards the upper lake goes into a border zone and may require a permit. A national park entrance fee applies.

name: Kaindy Lake (Sunken Forest)
description: Kaindy Lake is a narrow mountain lake about 400 m long at roughly 2,000 m above sea level. It formed after the 1911 Kebin earthquake caused a landslide that dammed a gorge and flooded a spruce forest. The bare trunks of the drowned spruce trees still stick out of the turquoise water, which makes the lake one of the most photographed places in Kazakhstan. In winter the lake freezes and ice divers visit it.
how_to_get_there: From Saty village a rough dirt road (about 12 km) leads to the lake; it is best done by 4x4 or on local hired off-road vehicles. The last part is a short walk downhill to the shore. Usually visited together with Kolsai Lakes.
tips: Ordinary city cars often cannot pass the road after rain, so hire a local 4x4 in Saty. The walk back up from the lake is steep. Bring a camera: the best light is in the morning.

name: Big Almaty Lake
description: Big Almaty Lake is a turquoise alpine lake at about 2,500 m above sea level in Ile-Alatau National Park, south of Almaty. The colour of the water changes during the year from light green to deep blue. The lake is a reservoir that supplies drinking water to Almaty, so swimming is not allowed. Above the lake there is the Tien Shan Astronomical Observatory and trails to higher peaks.
how_to_get_there: About 1-1.5 hours by taxi or car from the centre of Almaty through the Big Almaty Gorge. The last part of the road can be closed to private cars, in which case visitors walk or use park transport.
tips: Access is sometimes restricted by the park or border service, so check the current rules before going. It is much colder than in the city; take a jacket. Swimming and drones may be prohibited. Altitude can cause headaches for some people, so move slowly.

name: Medeu Skating Rink
description: Medeu is an outdoor high-altitude ice skating rink at about 1,690 m above sea level, opened in 1972 in a mountain valley above Almaty. Many speed skating world records were set here in Soviet times thanks to the thin air and pure glacier water used for the ice. Today it is a popular public skating rink in winter and a concert and event venue. A gondola connects Medeu with the Shymbulak ski resort.
how_to_get_there: City bus or taxi from the centre of Almaty takes about 30 minutes along Gornaya street (Medeu road).
tips: Public skating sessions run in the cold season (usually from late autumn to early spring); skates can be rented on site. Evening sessions with lights and music are popular. Combine with a gondola ride up to Shymbulak.

name: Shymbulak Ski Resort
description: Shymbulak is the largest and best-known ski resort in Central Asia, located in the Zailiysky Alatau mountains above Almaty. The slopes range from about 2,200 m to the Talgar Pass at roughly 3,200 m. A modern gondola runs from Medeu to the resort, and chairlifts go higher to the Talgar Pass. In summer the lifts work for sightseeing and hiking with panoramic views of the mountains.
how_to_get_there: Take a bus or taxi to Medeu (about 30 minutes from central Almaty), then the gondola up to Shymbulak.
tips: Ski season usually runs from December to April. Weekends are crowded, so buy lift passes online if possible. Equipment rental, ski schools, hotels and restaurants are available at the resort. Prices are higher than in the city.

name: Kok-Tobe Hill
description: Kok-Tobe ('Green Hill') is a hill on the south-eastern edge of Almaty at about 1,100 m above sea level, crowned by the city's TV tower. From the top there are panoramic views over Almaty and the mountains. The summit has a small amusement park, cafes, a mini-zoo and a monument to The Beatles. It is especially popular at sunset and in the evening when the city lights come on.
how_to_get_there: A cable car runs from the city centre (near Abay Avenue, next to the Palace of the Republic) to the top in about 6 minutes. You can also go up by taxi or by bus to the lower station and take the shuttle.
tips: Go about an hour before sunset to see the city in daylight and at night. Cable car queues are long on weekends. Bring a light jacket, it is windier on the hill.

name: Almaty City Centre: Panfilov Park, Zenkov Cathedral and Green Bazaar
description: The historic centre of Almaty is easy to explore on foot. Panfilov Park contains the Ascension (Zenkov) Cathedral, a colourful wooden Orthodox cathedral completed in 1907 that survived the strong 1911 earthquake. Nearby is the Green Bazaar (Zelyony Bazaar), the city's main market, where you can try dried fruits, nuts, horse-meat sausage (kazy), kurt and kumys. The pedestrian Arbat (Zhibek Zholy street) has street musicians and souvenir shops.
how_to_get_there: All three places are within walking distance of each other in central Almaty. The Zhibek Zholy metro station is next to the Arbat.
tips: The bazaar is busiest in the morning; ask for a taste before buying. Dress modestly when entering the cathedral. Combine with the Central State Museum and the Museum of Kazakh Folk Musical Instruments in Panfilov Park.

name: Assy Plateau
description: The Assy Plateau is a wide high-mountain plateau at about 2,500-2,800 m above sea level east of Almaty. In summer shepherds bring their herds here and set up yurts, so you can see a traditional nomadic lifestyle, horses and endless green meadows. The Assy-Turgen astronomical observatory is located on the plateau, and the clear sky makes it a great place for stargazing. The area also has ancient burial mounds and petroglyphs.
how_to_get_there: Through the Turgen Gorge: about 2.5-3 hours from Almaty, the last part on a rough mountain road suitable for 4x4 vehicles. Many agencies run one-day jeep tours.
tips: The road is usually passable only from June to September. Bring warm clothes for the evening and sun protection for the day. If you camp, ask shepherds before setting up near their yurts.

name: Turgen Gorge and Waterfalls
description: The Turgen Gorge lies in the foothills of the Zailiysky Alatau east of Almaty. It is known for several waterfalls, such as the Bear Waterfall and the Bozgul (Kairak) waterfall, which can be reached by short hikes. The valley has trout farms where you can catch and eat fresh fish, small guest houses and picnic spots along the river. It is a good, easy day trip for families.
how_to_get_there: About 1.5 hours by car from Almaty along the road towards Kegen, then turn south into the gorge. Some waterfalls require a 30-60 minute walk from the parking area.
tips: There is a small entrance fee to the gorge as part of the national park. Paths to waterfalls are slippery after rain. Try the local trout restaurants.

name: Tamgaly Petroglyphs
description: Tamgaly is an archaeological landscape in the Chu-Ili Mountains with around 5,000 rock carvings (petroglyphs), most of them from the Bronze Age (second half of the 2nd millennium BC). The carvings show sun-headed deities, animals, hunting scenes and rituals. Tamgaly was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2004 as 'Petroglyphs within the Archaeological Landscape of Tamgaly'.
how_to_get_there: About 2.5-3 hours by car north-west of Almaty; the last part is on a gravel road. There is no public transport, so go with a tour or a driver.
tips: There is a small visitor centre and marked paths. In summer it is very hot and there are snakes, so wear closed shoes and bring water. Do not touch or scratch the carvings.

name: Issyk Kurgans and the Golden Man
description: Near the town of Esik (Issyk) east of Almaty there is a field of ancient Saka burial mounds (kurgans). In 1969-1970 archaeologists found here the 'Golden Man': the remains of a young Saka warrior dressed in clothes decorated with thousands of gold plates, dating to around the 4th-3rd century BC. The Golden Man became one of the national symbols of Kazakhstan; a copy stands on top of the Independence Monument in Almaty. A museum next to the kurgans displays finds and replicas.
how_to_get_there: About 1 hour by car or intercity bus from Almaty (Sayakhat bus station) to the town of Esik.
tips: Combine with a visit to Issyk Lake in the mountains above the town. Check museum opening hours in advance; museums are often closed on Mondays.

name: Altyn-Emel National Park (Singing Dunes)
description: Altyn-Emel is a large national park between the Ili River and the Dzungarian Alatau. Its highlights are the Singing Dune, a sand dune about 150 m high and 3 km long that hums in dry windy weather; the Aktau and Katutau mountains with bright white, red and orange layers of clay; and the Besshatyr Saka burial mounds. Wild kulans (Asian wild asses) and goitered gazelles live in the park.
how_to_get_there: About 4 hours by car from Almaty. The park office is in the village of Basshi, where you buy permits and can stay in guest houses. Distances inside the park are long (the sights are 100+ km apart), so a 4x4 is strongly recommended.
tips: A permit from the park administration is required and is usually bought in Basshi. Plan two days to see the dune and the Aktau mountains. Carry enough water and fuel. Avoid the hottest summer months.

name: Kapchagay Reservoir (Konaev)
description: The Kapchagay Reservoir is a large artificial lake on the Ili River north of Almaty. The town on its shore, formerly called Kapchagay, was renamed Konaev in 2022. In summer the reservoir is the closest beach destination for Almaty residents, with sandy beaches, rest zones, water sports and cafes.
how_to_get_there: About 1-1.5 hours by car or intercity bus from Almaty.
tips: Summer weekends are crowded. Choose an organised beach zone with facilities. Bring sun protection: there is little shade.

name: Zharkent Mosque
description: The Zharkent Mosque was built in 1887-1892 by the Chinese architect Hon Pik and combines Chinese pagoda-style architecture with traditional Central Asian Islamic elements. It was built of wood without nails on a brick base and has a minaret that looks like a Chinese tower. Today it is an architectural and art museum and one of the most unusual buildings in Kazakhstan.
how_to_get_there: Zharkent is about 5 hours by car or bus from Almaty, close to the border with China. It can be combined with a trip to Altyn-Emel.
tips: Visitors should dress modestly. Photography inside may require a small extra fee.

name: Lake Alakol
description: Alakol is a large salt lake in eastern Kazakhstan. Its slightly salty, mineral-rich water is considered healing for skin and joints, which made it one of the most popular summer beach destinations in the country. The resort villages Koktuma, Akshi and Kabanbay have many guest houses and resort hotels. The lake is also part of a nature reserve important for migrating birds.
how_to_get_there: Seasonal trains from Almaty or Astana go to Koktuma/Beskol stations in summer. By car it is about 9-10 hours from Almaty.
tips: The season is short (roughly late June to August), so book train tickets and accommodation early. It is often windy. Shower after swimming because of the salt.

name: Lake Balkhash
description: Lake Balkhash is one of the largest lakes in Asia, about 600 km long. Its unique feature is that the western part is almost fresh water while the eastern part is salty; the two parts are connected by a narrow strait. The town of Balkhash on the northern shore has beaches and rest zones, and the lake is popular for summer holidays and fishing.
how_to_get_there: The town of Balkhash has a railway station on the Almaty-Astana line and a small airport. By car it is about 7-8 hours from Almaty or Karaganda.
tips: The water warms up well in July and August. Shores are often windy and there are mosquitoes in the evening. Rest zones along the shore offer simple cottages.

name: Astana: Baiterek and Modern Architecture
description: Astana has been the capital of Kazakhstan since 1997 and is famous for its futuristic architecture. The Baiterek tower is the symbol of the city: its observation sphere is at a height of 97 m, a reference to 1997. Other landmarks include the Khan Shatyr entertainment centre (a giant transparent tent), the Hazrat Sultan Mosque, the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation (a pyramid designed by Norman Foster), the National Museum of Kazakhstan and the Nur Alem sphere left from EXPO-2017.
how_to_get_there: Astana has an international airport and is connected by trains with all major cities. Within the city, use buses or taxi apps; the new LRT line is being developed.
tips: Winters are very cold (often below -25 C) and windy, so summer and early autumn are the most comfortable for walking. The main sights lie along the central Nurzhol Boulevard axis, which is pleasant to walk in the evening when buildings are lit up.

name: Burabay National Park (Borovoe)
description: Burabay, often called the 'Kazakh Switzerland', is a resort area of pine forests, clear lakes and granite rocks in the middle of the steppe. Its symbols are the Okzhetpes rock ('the arrow will not reach') and the Zhumbaktas ('mysterious stone') rising from Lake Burabay, both connected with Kazakh legends. The area has many hotels and sanatoriums, walking trails and the Blue Bay (Golubaya Bukhta) beach.
how_to_get_there: About 3 hours by car from Astana. Trains run from Astana to Burabay (Borovoe) or Shchuchinsk stations, followed by a short taxi ride.
tips: Book hotels early for summer weekends and holidays. A national park eco-fee is charged at the entrance. In winter there is cross-country skiing and a small ski slope.

name: Karkaraly National Park
description: Karkaraly National Park protects a group of low granite mountains covered in pine forest that rise from the Kazakh steppe. The park has bizarre rock formations, the small Shaitankol lake high in the mountains, caves and many hiking trails. The historic town of Karkaraly at the foot of the mountains was a trading centre in the 19th century.
how_to_get_there: About 3-4 hours by car or bus from Karaganda.
tips: Accommodation is mostly in rest houses and guest houses around the town. Bring tick protection in late spring and early summer.

name: Bayanaul National Park
description: Bayanaul, created in 1985, is the oldest national park in Kazakhstan. It is a mountain oasis in the steppe with pine forests, granite rocks of strange shapes (such as the 'Stone Head' and 'Konyrauliye' cave) and several lakes: Zhasybai, Sabyndykol and Toraigyr. Lake Zhasybai is the most popular summer swimming spot with many rest zones.
how_to_get_there: About 3.5-4 hours by bus or car from Pavlodar, or from Ekibastuz which is closer.
tips: The water in the lakes is clean but cool. The summer season is short (July-August). Book rest-zone cottages in advance.

name: Karlag Museum in Dolinka
description: Karlag (Karaganda Corrective Labour Camp) was one of the largest camps of the Soviet Gulag system, operating from 1931 to 1959. In the village of Dolinka, in the former administration building of the camp, there is the Museum of Memory of Victims of Political Repression. The exhibitions tell the stories of prisoners, including many deported people and scientists, and include reconstructed cells and interrogation rooms in the basement.
how_to_get_there: About 45 minutes by car or taxi from Karaganda.
tips: A guided tour is recommended to understand the history; ask about tours in English or Russian in advance. The exhibition is emotionally heavy and may not be suitable for small children.

name: Ulytau Mountains
description: Ulytau ('Great Mountain') is a low mountain range in the very centre of Kazakhstan, considered a sacred place and the cradle of Kazakh statehood. Here are the mausoleums of Zhoshy Khan (Jochi), the eldest son of Genghis Khan, and Alasha Khan, as well as many ancient monuments and burial sites. In 2022 a new Ulytau Region was created with its centre in Zhezkazgan.
how_to_get_there: Fly or take a train to Zhezkazgan, then about 2 hours by car to Ulytau village. The monuments are spread out, so a car with a driver or a tour is needed.
tips: Infrastructure is basic; stay in Zhezkazgan or in guest houses in Ulytau village. Bring water and food for trips across the steppe.

name: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi (Turkistan)
description: The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkistan was commissioned by Timur (Tamerlane) in 1389 over the grave of the 12th-century Sufi poet and mystic Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, and remained unfinished after Timur's death. Its huge turquoise dome and tiled walls are a masterpiece of Timurid architecture. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003 and is the most important pilgrimage site in Kazakhstan. The city around it has a new tourist centre, Karavansaray, with shops and an evening show.
how_to_get_there: Turkistan has an international airport (opened in 2020) and a railway station with direct trains from Almaty, Astana and Shymkent. From Shymkent it is about 2.5 hours by car.
tips: Dress modestly: covered shoulders and knees, women may be asked to cover their heads. Spring and autumn are best; summer temperatures often exceed 40 C. Combine with Arystan Bab, Otrar and Sauran.

name: Otrar Ruins and Arystan Bab Mausoleum
description: Otrar was a major Silk Road city on the Syr Darya. In 1219 an incident with a Mongol trade caravan at Otrar triggered Genghis Khan's invasion of Central Asia, and the city was destroyed. Today visitors can walk on the excavated hill (tobe) of the ancient city. Nearby stands the Mausoleum of Arystan Bab, the teacher of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi; by tradition pilgrims visit Arystan Bab before going to Yasawi's mausoleum in Turkistan.
how_to_get_there: About 1 hour by car from Turkistan. Usually visited as part of a day tour from Turkistan or Shymkent.
tips: There is little shade at the ruins; bring a hat and water. There is a small museum in the village of Shauildir.

name: Sauran Ancient City
description: Sauran is the ruins of a medieval fortified city north-west of Turkistan, mentioned in sources from the 10th century and once a capital of the White Horde. Its oval clay walls, several metres high, are still well visible from the road, which makes it one of the best-preserved ancient cities in Kazakhstan. The site also had an underground water system called kariz.
how_to_get_there: About 40 minutes by car from Turkistan along the Turkistan-Kyzylorda highway.
tips: Best visited in the early morning or at sunset for photos. There are no facilities at the site, so bring water.

name: Shymkent City
description: Shymkent is the third-largest city of Kazakhstan and the centre of the warm south. It is known for its friendly atmosphere, rich southern cuisine (lagman, samsa, plov, shashlik) and lively bazaars. Main sights include Ordabasy Square, the Independence Park with the ethno-park, Dendropark and the Shymkent Plaza area. Shymkent is a convenient base for trips to Turkistan, Sairam and Aksu-Zhabagly.
how_to_get_there: Shymkent has an international airport and good train and bus connections with Almaty (about 10-12 hours by train), Astana and Tashkent (about 2 hours by car).
tips: Prices for food and hotels are lower than in Almaty and Astana. Summers are very hot. Visit the ancient town of Sairam nearby, one of the oldest settlements in Kazakhstan.

name: Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve
description: Aksu-Zhabagly, established in 1926, is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia, located in the Western Tien Shan. It is famous for wild tulips, especially Greig's tulip, which bloom in April and May, for the deep Aksu canyon, and for wildlife such as ibex, argali, bears and many birds. The reserve is part of the Western Tien Shan UNESCO World Heritage site.
how_to_get_there: About 2 hours by car from Shymkent to the village of Zhabagly, where there are guest houses that organise visits with rangers.
tips: Entering a strict nature reserve requires permission and usually an official guide; guest houses in Zhabagly help arrange this. The best time for flowers is mid-April to May.

name: Taraz and Aisha Bibi Mausoleum
description: Taraz is one of the oldest cities in Kazakhstan, which officially celebrated its 2000th anniversary in 2002. West of the city stands the Aisha Bibi Mausoleum (11th-12th century), decorated with fine carved terracotta tiles with more than 60 different patterns. According to legend, it was built by a ruler for his beloved Aisha Bibi, who died on the way to their wedding. Next to it is the mausoleum of her nanny, Babaji Khatun. The mausoleum is a popular place for newlyweds.
how_to_get_there: Taraz is on the railway between Almaty and Shymkent. The mausoleum is in the village of Aisha Bibi, about 20 minutes by taxi from the centre.
tips: In Taraz visit also the Karakhan Mausoleum and the ancient settlement museum. A visit takes about 2-3 hours.

name: Baikonur Cosmodrome
description: Baikonur is the world's first and largest space launch facility. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin started the first human spaceflight from here, and the launch pad is known as 'Gagarin's Start'. The cosmodrome and the city of Baikonur are leased by Russia from Kazakhstan, and crewed Soyuz missions to the International Space Station still launch from here. The site has a museum of cosmonautics and the house-museums of Gagarin and Korolev.
how_to_get_there: Visits are only possible with an organised tour that arranges a special access permit in advance (often 1-2 months ahead). Tours usually travel via Kyzylorda or by charter flight to Baikonur.
tips: Launch tours are expensive and limited, so book early. You cannot visit the cosmodrome independently. Bring your passport; permits are checked strictly.

name: Aral Sea and the Ship Graveyard of Aralsk
description: The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the world, but it shrank dramatically from the 1960s because rivers were used for irrigation, which is considered one of the worst ecological disasters of the 20th century. The former port town of Aralsk now lies far from the water, and rusting fishing ships can be seen in the dried seabed near the villages of Zhalanash. After the Kokaral Dam was finished in 2005, the North (Small) Aral Sea started to recover and fishing returned.
how_to_get_there: Aralsk is on the railway between Kyzylorda and Aktobe. From Aralsk, trips to the ships and to the current shoreline require a 4x4 and a local guide.
tips: Visit the Aral Sea museum in Aralsk to understand the history. Roads to the ships are unpaved. Summer is very hot and dusty.

name: Aktau and the Caspian Sea Coast
description: Aktau is a city on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea and the main gateway to the Mangystau region. It is unusual because instead of street names it uses numbered micro-districts. Visitors come for the rocky Caspian coast, the embankment with sunset views, sandy beaches south of the city and as a starting point for desert trips to Bozzhyra, Sherkala and the underground mosques.
how_to_get_there: Aktau has an international airport with flights from Almaty and Astana. Trains run from other regions to Mangyshlak station near the city.
tips: Plan desert trips from Aktau with a local tour operator, as distances are long and roads are rough. The sea is warm enough for swimming from late June to September.

name: Bozzhyra Valley (Mangystau)
description: Bozzhyra is a dramatic valley on the edge of the Ustyurt Plateau with white limestone cliffs and two sharp peaks that are often called the 'fangs'. The landscape looks like another planet: millions of years ago this was the bottom of the ancient Tethys Ocean, and fossil shells can still be found. It is considered one of the most beautiful places in Kazakhstan and is ideal for photography and camping under the stars.
how_to_get_there: Only reachable by 4x4 on desert tracks: several hours' drive from Aktau via Zhanaozen. Most travellers join a 2-3 day jeep tour that combines Bozzhyra, Tuzbair salt flat and Beket-Ata.
tips: There is no mobile signal, water, or shops at the site; travel with an experienced driver. Spring and autumn are best; summer can exceed 40 C. Do not drive to the cliff edges.

name: Sherkala Mountain and Torysh Valley of Balls
description: Sherkala ('Lion Fortress') is a lonely white mountain near the village of Shetpe that, depending on the angle, resembles a lying lion or a yurt. Legends connect it with an ancient fortress. Not far away lies the Torysh Valley, also called the Valley of Balls, where hundreds of almost perfectly round stone balls (geological concretions) of different sizes are scattered across the steppe.
how_to_get_there: About 3 hours by car from Aktau via Shetpe. A day tour from Aktau usually combines Sherkala, Torysh and the Shakpak-Ata underground mosque.
tips: Roads near the sites are unpaved; a 4x4 is better. Do not take stones from the Valley of Balls.

name: Beket-Ata Underground Mosque
description: Beket-Ata is an underground mosque carved into a chalk cliff in the Oglandy area, where the Sufi teacher and healer Beket-Ata (18th century) lived and taught. It is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in western Kazakhstan. Pilgrims usually first visit the Shopan-Ata underground necropolis and mosque on the way, and stay overnight in the free pilgrim house near the site.
how_to_get_there: From Aktau via Zhanaozen; the last part is a desert road. Pilgrim buses and tours go from Aktau and Zhanaozen. The walk from the parking area down to the mosque takes about 20-30 minutes.
tips: It is a sacred place: dress modestly and behave respectfully. Women should cover their heads. The walk back up to the parking area is steep, so bring water.

name: Kiin-Kerish Flaming Cliffs
description: Kiin-Kerish, known as the 'Flaming Cliffs', is an area of bright red, orange and white clay formations near Lake Zaisan in East Kazakhstan. At sunset the cliffs seem to glow like fire. The site is also important for paleontology: fossils of ancient plants and animals have been found in its layers.
how_to_get_there: Reach the town of Zaisan (about 8 hours from Ust-Kamenogorsk / Oskemen), then drive on unpaved roads with a 4x4 and a local guide.
tips: The clay is fragile; stay on paths and do not climb the formations. Visit at sunset for the best colours.

name: Katon-Karagay National Park and Rakhmanov Springs
description: Katon-Karagay is the largest national park in Kazakhstan, created in 2001 in the Kazakh Altai mountains. It is famous for alpine meadows, larch and cedar forests, waterfalls and maral deer farms. In the park lies the Rakhmanov Springs (Rakhmanovskiye Klyuchi), a resort with warm radon mineral springs next to a mountain lake, which is also a starting point for treks towards Mount Belukha (4,506 m), the highest peak of the Altai on the border with Russia.
how_to_get_there: From Ust-Kamenogorsk (Oskemen) it is a long drive (8-10 hours) to the village of Katon-Karagay; Rakhmanov Springs requires an additional off-road trip by 4x4.
tips: Large parts of the area are a border zone: you need a border permit arranged in advance (usually through a tour operator). The season is short, mainly July-August. Weather in the mountains changes quickly.

name: Lake Markakol
description: Markakol is a large mountain lake in the Southern Altai at about 1,450 m above sea level, surrounded by taiga forest. It is protected by the Markakol State Nature Reserve. The lake is known for its clean water, the endemic uskuch fish (Markakol lenok) and wild, untouched nature with almost no tourist infrastructure.
how_to_get_there: From Ust-Kamenogorsk (Oskemen) via Kurchum and Alekseevka by car; the last part is a mountain road. The trip takes most of a day.
tips: Accommodation is limited to a few guest houses in nearby villages. Visiting the reserve may require permission from the reserve administration. Mosquitoes are common in summer.

name: Sibiny Lakes
description: The Sibiny Lakes are a group of five small lakes among granite rocks in the Kalba mountains of East Kazakhstan. The clear water and smooth, oddly shaped rocks make it a favourite summer weekend destination for people from Ust-Kamenogorsk (Oskemen), with simple rest zones, camping and swimming.
how_to_get_there: About 2-2.5 hours by car from Ust-Kamenogorsk (Oskemen); the last part is a gravel road.
tips: Book a cottage in a rest zone in advance for July weekends, or bring a tent. Water is cool even in summer.

name: Practical info: visas, money and mobile internet
description: Citizens of many countries can visit Kazakhstan without a visa for a limited period (often up to 30 days); rules depend on citizenship, so always check the official migration service or embassy website before travelling. The local currency is the tenge (KZT). Bank cards are accepted almost everywhere in cities, while cash is useful in villages, bazaars and national parks. Local SIM cards with mobile internet are cheap and can be bought at the airport or in shops with a passport.
tips: Useful apps: 2GIS for maps and public transport, Yandex Go for taxis, and the national railway app/website for train tickets. ATMs are widely available in cities. Keep some cash for park entrance fees.

name: Practical info: getting around Kazakhstan
description: Kazakhstan is the ninth-largest country in the world, so distances are huge. Domestic flights connect Almaty, Astana, Shymkent, Turkistan, Aktau and other cities and save a lot of time. Trains are cheap and comfortable, with overnight sleeper cars on long routes; tickets are sold online by the national railway company. For nature sites near Almaty, most travellers use tours or hire a car with a driver, because public transport to parks is limited.
tips: Book trains early in summer and on holidays. For the mountains, Charyn or Mangystau, an off-road vehicle with an experienced driver is safer than driving yourself. Taxi apps work in all big cities.

name: Practical info: Kazakh food and hospitality
description: Kazakh cuisine is based on meat and dairy from nomadic traditions. The national dish is beshbarmak: boiled meat (often horse meat or lamb) served on flat noodles with onion broth. Other dishes include kazy (horse-meat sausage), baursak (fried dough pieces), kurt (dried salty cheese balls), kumys (fermented mare's milk) and shubat (fermented camel's milk). Tea with milk is served all the time. Hospitality is very important: guests are invited to the dastarkhan (a richly laid table) and are offered the best food.
tips: If you are invited to a home, bring a small gift and take off your shoes at the entrance. It is polite to accept at least some tea. Kumys and shubat are strong for an unused stomach, so try small amounts first. Nauryz (21-23 March) is the spring holiday with special food like nauryz kozhe.

name: Practical info: safety in mountains and nature
description: Mountain weather in Kazakhstan changes quickly, so bring warm and waterproof clothes even in summer. In spring and early summer (roughly April to June) ticks are active in forests and grasslands of the south-east and east, and some can carry tick-borne encephalitis, so use repellent and check your body after hikes. At altitudes above 2,500 m some people get altitude sickness. Many national parks charge entrance fees, and areas near the borders with China and Kyrgyzstan may require a border-zone permit.
tips: Tell someone your route before hiking. The emergency number in Kazakhstan is 112. Avalanche danger is high in the mountains in late winter and spring. Hire certified guides for serious trekking.
